It supported REECo, a long-time contractor that provided extensive administrative support for many day-to-day site operations during the period of significance for the Control Point, as well as EG&G, which provided direct technical support to the national laboratories. Beginning in the 1970s, the building was important in providing power and a staging area for many diagnostic instrumentation trailers that were a vital piece of equipment for underground testing. Its location, just adjacent to Mercury Highway reminds the viewer of the importance of this building’s mission to support diagnostic trailers and the importance of the Control Point’s easy accessibility in the forward area of the NNSS. The building also contributes to the historic district under Criterion C as it is one of the large, unadorned, precast concrete buildings at the Control Point. These types of buildings were prominent architectural elements of the compound and add to the district’s overall utilitarian, military- industrial character. This warehouse retains all aspects of integrity and easily conveys its significance as a warehouse that supported Control Point operations. It is eligible for listing in the NRHP as a contributing element to the Area 6 Control Point Historic District as a result. Narrative Architectural Description Provide a detailed description of the resource, including all character defining features, potential construction methods, potential alterations (both historic and non-historic), and any accessory resources. This is a concrete warehouse on the east side of the Area 6 Control Point Historic District, just west of Mercury Highway. It is a 350 × 100 ft. one story rectangular plan building with precast concrete wall panels. The built-up roof sits on concrete and metal decking and has a sheet metal fascia. The roof is nearly flat with a very low pitch to accommodate proper drainage. Installed along the length of the roof is HVAC equipment. The front of the building (east elevation) is designed to allow access for loading trailers. On this elevation are four pairs of pedestrian double doors and a single, metal-framed window opening infilled with small metal doors. It served as the “issue window” for communications between staff inside and outside the building (see elevation drawing in Section 13). Painted on this elevation’s wall are yellow stenciled numbers from 1 to 14, designating loading stall numbers. In front of this elevation is a cast-in-place loading dock that extends the length of the building. On the right side of the north elevation is another set of pedestrian double doors and a large roll-up loading door. A roof access ladder is on the left side of this elevation. The south elevation has a single set of pedestrian double doors inset from the building’s exterior wall plane.
